newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmenistan marks birthdays of leader, flag.
newsitem.headline: Turkmenistan marks birthdays of leader, flag.

text.p: Turkmenistan staged elaborate festivities on Wednesday to celebrate the 57th birthday of its leader Saparmurat Niyazov, who enjoys a Soviet-style personality cult in this impoverished Central Asian country.
Niyazov's birthday coincided this year with the Day of the National Flag in Turkmenistan, listed among the poorest post-socialist states.
The former Soviet republic with a population of some four million people held pompous events to mark both holidays.
The Turkmen capital Ashgabat hosted a military parade on its central square, named Saparmurat Turkmenbashi after Niyazov, whose official title Turkmenbashi means "head of the Turkmen."
Ashgabat also held races of the desert nation's famous Akhal-Teke horses and the final of the Turkmenbashi Football Cup with a prize fund of $125,000.

Birthday celebrations for Niyazov, who was Turkmenistan's communist-era boss, overshadowed the festivities devoted to the national flag, the symbol of independence gained after the overnight collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991.
Companies doing business in Turkmenistan competed with one another to honour Niyazov, who is fond of saying "I was only 12 when I felt I would become president".
A dairy factory in Ashgabat started producing yoghurts with his face on every pack.

A spokesman for Dutch company Royal Sluis, which trades flowers among other interests, said the company had selected a variety of dahlia and named it Turkmenbashi (the head of Turmen) as a gift for Niyazov from a group of local and foreign firms.
The president is said to be planning to plant these dahlias around a new luxurious mansion being built for him in central Ashgabat.

Niyazov's name is already borne by nearly everything in Turkmenistan, from an anti-aircraft brigade to the town of Turkmenbashi on the Caspian coast and his face appears on every banknote of the manat currency.
Monuments to him have been erected in every town and most of the villages and his gold-plated profile greets every foreigner arriving at the Ashgabat International Airport bearing his name.
Niyazov's presidency was extended until the year 2002 by a referendum in January 1994. Officials said over 90 percent of voters had backed the decision.
Niyazov has promised his nation, whose monthly wages average a mere $18, "10 years of stability".

Turkmenis have to endure bread rationing and lack of freedom. But opposition to Niyazov -- head of the government, commander-in-chief of the armed forces and signatory of all commercial deals worth more than $1 million -- is weak.
Many people seem tired by everyday hardships, while some still believe official promises that resource-rich Turkmenistan will become another Kuwait.
